questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are symmetric?

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${p}_{12}\ne {p}_{21},$ we obtain $P\ne {P}^{T}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- $Q$ is a symmetric matrix. Indeed, $Q={Q}^{T}.$

- $R$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${r}_{12}\ne {r}_{21},$ we obtain $R\ne {R}^{T}.$

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$Q$ only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then ${A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.

II. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.

III. If $A$ is a symmetric matrix, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

However, ${A}^{2}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Which of the following statements are true? 

I. If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.

II. The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A{A}^{T})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =A{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Example: 
                    Identifying True Statements Regarding Properties of Symmetric Matrices
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

II. The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A square matrix $A$ is **symmetric** if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A^T = A
$$

Equivalently, an $n\times n$ matrix is symmetric if $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $1 \leq i,j\leq n.$

If $A$ is symmetric, this really means that it is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

For example, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/0f62a89f8da1ab7bfb86d46fddb441e95e5e3a9554e5a88662691b4df40e19af.svg)

is symmetric since $A^T = A.$ 

On the other hand, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/780de3c3f66b1037e4152224f4aa98b65b8b1b859adfe7c3881bb830d7eecd66.svg)

is not symmetric. Indeed, since $b_{12} \neq b_{21},$ we have $B^T \neq B.$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
A square matrix $A$ is **symmetric** if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A^T = A
$$

Equivalently, an $n\times n$ matrix is symmetric if $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $1 \leq i,j\leq n.$

If $A$ is symmetric, this really means that it is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

For example, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/0f62a89f8da1ab7bfb86d46fddb441e95e5e3a9554e5a88662691b4df40e19af.svg)

is symmetric since $A^T = A.$ 

On the other hand, the matrix 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/780de3c3f66b1037e4152224f4aa98b65b8b1b859adfe7c3881bb830d7eecd66.svg)

is not symmetric. Indeed, since $b_{12} \neq b_{21},$ we have $B^T \neq B.$

tutorials.name: Properties of Symmetric Matrices
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14166469/assets/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

- $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are symmetric for *any* matrix $A$

The last property is true for *any* $m\times n$ matrix. This property is particularly useful, as we'll discover in future lessons.
